parts: Human wants are unlimited, and they are satisfied by goods and services. Goods are things like food, pens, chairs, houses and television sets. Services are the work of people such as a hairdresser, doctor, tailor or cobbler. Both goods and services satisfy human wants.

Goods are tangible: they can be seen and touched. There is a time gap between their production and consumption, since a chair is made first and used later. Goods can be stored and used when needed, and they can be transferred from one place or person to another.

Services are non-tangible: they cannot be seen or touched. There is no time gap between production and consumption. A service is produced and consumed at the same time, as when a doctor examines a patient. Services cannot be stored, and they cannot be transferred.
Free goods are free gifts of nature, such as air, sunlight, or sand in a desert. Their supply is more than their demand, so they have utility but are not scarce and have no price.

Economic goods are scarce, because their demand is more than their supply. So they command a price and are bought in the market. They may be man-made (soap, bread, machines) or gifts of nature that have become scarce (water, sand in a city, minerals).

Free services cannot be bought in the market. They are given out of love and affection, such as a parent's care or a mother cooking dinner. Economic services are bought in the market, such as the services of doctors, engineers and lawyers.

This classification is based on the purpose for which a good is used. Consumer goods satisfy wants directly, like bread, fruit, milk and clothes. Producer goods satisfy wants indirectly by helping to produce other goods, like machinery, tools, raw materials, seeds, manure and tractors. Intermediate goods are raw materials, power and fuel used to produce final goods; for example, wheat flour is an intermediate good for a bakery.

Consumer services are used directly by households: a tailor stitching your shirt, a doctor treating you, a plumber fixing your tap. Producer services help produce other goods and services: a tailor stitching shirts for a garment shop, an electrician repairing a factory's wiring, a truck carrying raw material to a factory.

Single-use goods are finished in one use. Single-use consumer goods include bread, butter, eggs and milk. Single-use producer goods include coal, raw material, seeds and manure; sugarcane, for example, is used up in making sugar. Durable-use goods are used again and again for a long time. Durable consumer goods include clothes, furniture, TV sets and scooters; durable producer goods include machines, tools and tractors. Durable goods lose value (depreciate) with continued use.

This classification is based on ownership. Private goods are owned and enjoyed exclusively by individuals, such as your watch, pen, scooter, or the machinery of your factory. Public goods are owned and enjoyed by society as a whole, such as roads, bridges, parks and town halls. They are available to all without discrimination. Both the government and private entrepreneurs may produce public goods.
Human wants: more goods and services satisfy more wants.
Production: the supply of consumer goods depends on the quantity and quality of producer goods and services (machines, seeds, transport, banking).
Investment: the part of production that is not consumed is used for further production, which is capital formation. The larger the surplus, the larger the productive capacity of the economy.
